title: Chapter 40: The Stalk of Grass 8
content:
Chapter 40

Any other girl her age would have screamed her lungs out. But A-Qing had played the blind girl for years. People assumed she couldn't see, which meant they never bothered hiding their ugliness around her. She had seen too much, suffered too much, and grown nerves of steel because of it. She didn't make a peep.

Still, Wei Wuxian could feel the cold, prickling numbness creeping straight up her legs.

Xiao Xingchen stood among the sprawled, tangled bodies of the villagers. He sheathed his sword, his expression grim. “Not a single survivor in the whole village? Were they all walking corpses?”

A smirk curled the corner of Xue Yang’s lips, though the voice that came out of his mouth was laced with pure shock and a touch of grief. “Afraid so. Thank goodness your sword points right to the corpse energy, Daozhang. Just the two of us? We barely would’ve made it out alive.”

“Let’s sweep the village one more time,” Xiao Xingchen said quietly. “If no one is left alive, we need to burn these corpses as soon as possible.”

Only after the two walked away side-by-side did the feeling finally flood back into A-Qing’s legs. Slipping out from behind the cottage, she crept over to the heap of dead bodies, peering down to inspect them left and right. Wei Wuxian’s vision drifted along with hers.

Every single villager had been struck down cleanly—one fatal thrust through the heart by Xiao Xingchen’s blade. Suddenly, Wei Wuxian caught sight of a few vaguely familiar faces.

Just a few memories ago, the three of them had been out during the day and crossed paths with some idle loafers playing dice at a crossroads. As they passed, the loafers glanced up, bursting into crude laughter and pointing fingers at the sight of a blind man, a blind girl, and a crippled kid. A-Qing had spat at them and swung her bamboo pole; Xiao Xingchen had walked right past them with serene indifference, as if he hadn't heard a thing; and Xue Yang had even smiled. But his eyes hadn't held a flicker of amusement.

A-Qing checked several bodies in a row, peeling back their eyelids to reveal milky white pupils. A few faces were already mottled with dark corpse spots. She let out a breath of relief, but Wei Wuxian’s heart sank like a stone.

They might look like walking corpses,he realized with mounting dread,but they were living, breathing people.

They were just living people poisoned by corpse venom.

Around the mouths and noses of several bodies, Wei Wuxian spotted faint traces of a purplish-red powder. Those who were too far gone—reduced to mindless husks—were beyond saving. But those only lightly afflicted could still be pulled back from the brink. These villagers had only just been poisoned. They bore the outward signs of transformation and reeked of corpse energy, but they could still think, speak, and feel. They were alive. With the right medicine, just like Lan Jingyi and the other juniors, they could have been saved. Killing them was out of the question—it was flat-out slaughtering the innocent.

They could have spoken. They could have told Xiao Xingchen who they were, or begged for their lives. The horror of it was that every single one of them had had their tongue cut out beforehand. Fresh or dried blood trickled from the corner of every mouth.

Xiao Xingchen was blind, but Shuanghua guided him straight to the presence of corpse energy. Strip the villagers of their tongues, leave them moaning in agony like the undead, and he wouldn't doubt for a second that he was putting down monsters.

Vicious. Psychopathic. Murder by proxy.Returning boundless kindness with pure malice—it was utterly vile.

A-Qing didn't grasp any of this. What little she knew of cultivation came from bits and pieces Xiao Xingchen occasionally mentioned. She muttered under her breath, “Wait… is that creep actually helping Daozhang?”

Don’t you dare fall for it!Wei Wuxian shouted internally.

Fortunately, A-Qing’s instincts were razor-sharp. She might lack the worldly knowledge to spot the scheme, but her gut distrust of Xue Yang was bone-deep. She loathed him on principle and refused to let her guard down. From then on, whenever Xue Yang tagged along on night-hunts with Xiao Xingchen, she shadowed them in secret. Even under the same roof, she kept one eye open.

One winter night, the wind howled outside while the three of them huddled around a battered stove for warmth. Xiao Xingchen was busy patching a broken corner of a woven bamboo basket. A-Qing, wrapped up like a dumpling in their only cotton quilt, nestled close against him. Xue Yang rested his chin on his hand, bored out of his mind. Listening to A-Qing badger Xiao Xingchen for a bedtime story, he snapped, “Shut up already. Keep whining and I’ll tie your tongue in a knot.”

A-Qing ignored him completely. “Daozhang, tell me a story! Come on!”

“Nobody ever told me stories when I was little,” Xiao Xingchen said softly. “How am I supposed to tell you one?”

A-Qing kept pestering him, thrashing about as if ready to roll on the floor. Xiao Xingchen relented with a sigh. “All right, all right. I’ll tell you a story about a mountain.”

“Once upon a time, there was a mountain, and on the mountain was a temple?” A-Qing chimed in.

“No,” Xiao Xingchen corrected gently. “Once upon a time, there was an unnamed celestial mountain where an enlightened immortal lived. The immortal took in many disciples, but forbade them from ever descending the mountain.”

The moment the tale began, Wei Wuxian knew:Baoshan Sanren.

“Why weren't they allowed down?” A-Qing asked.

“Because the immortal herself didn't understand the secular world down below, which was why she fled to the mountain in the first place. She told her disciples: if you choose to leave, never return. Do not bring the outside world’s strife back to these peaks.”

“Who could stand that?” A-Qing scoffed. “Someone definitely snuck down to have some fun.”

“Indeed,” Xiao Xingchen replied. “The first to leave was an exceptional disciple. At first, his extraordinary skills earned him widespread admiration and praise, making him a celebrated cultivator of the righteous path. But later, something happened to him. His temperament shifted drastically, and he turned into a ruthless, bloodthirsty fiend. In the end, he was hacked to death by a mob.”

The first of Baoshan Sanren’s disciples to meet a tragic end: Daoist Yanling.

What had driven Wei Wuxian’s martial uncle to madness after descending into the mortal realm remained an enduring mystery. Likely, no one would ever know. Having smoothed down the rough bamboo splinters of the basket to make sure it wouldn't prick anyone, Xiao Xingchen set it down and continued, “The second disciple was also a brilliant young woman.”

Wei Wuxian’s chest tightened with sudden warmth.

Cangse Sanren.

“Was she pretty?” A-Qing asked.

“I don't know,” Xiao Xingchen smiled. “They say she was breathtaking.”

A-Qing cupped her cheeks. “Oh, I bet she was! I bet tons of men were head over heels for her, lining up to marry her! She must've married some high-ranking official, or a wealthy clan leader! Right?”

Xiao Xingchen chuckled. “Wrong guess. She married a clan leader’s servant, and the two of them ran off together.”

“Ugh, lame,” A-Qing groaned, wrinkling her nose. “Why would a gorgeous, talented fairy ever fall for a servant? That's so cliché—sounds like something a bunch of broke, bitter scholars dreamed up. What happened next? Did they live happily ever after?”

“Later, they both perished during a night-hunt gone wrong,” Xiao Xingchen said softly.

A-Qing spat in disgust. “What kind of garbage story is this?! Marrying a servant was bad enough, but dying together too? I'm done, I don't want to hear it!”

Wei Wuxian couldn't help but think:Good thing Xiao Xingchen didn't mention they also had a son who grew up to be a universally hated demon, or she’d probably spit in my face right now.

“See?” Xiao Xingchen said helplessly. “I told you from the start, I’m no storyteller.”

“Then talk about your own night-hunts, Daozhang! I love those!” A-Qing pressed eagerly. “Tell me, what kind of monsters have you fought?”

Xue Yang had been squinting into space, half-listening. At that question, his pupils constricted, and his gaze cut sideways toward Xiao Xingchen.

“Too many to count,” Xiao Xingchen murmured.

Suddenly, Xue Yang spoke up. “Is that so? Did Daozhang always hunt alone back then, too?”

A slight smirk played on Xue Yang’s lips—dripping with malice, yet his tone was polished with innocent curiosity. Xiao Xingchen paused, then offered a faint smile. “No.”

A-Qing’s ears perked up. “Who else was there?”

This time, Xiao Xingchen hesitated even longer. Only after a heavy silence did he say, “A very dear friend of mine.”

A sinister glint flickered in Xue Yang’s eyes, his smirk widening. Peeling back Xiao Xingchen’s old scars clearly brought him twisted pleasure. A-Qing, genuinely curious, asked, “What kind of person is he, Daozhang? What was he like?”

“A noble gentleman of absolute integrity,” Xiao Xingchen answered calmly.

Hearing this, Xue Yang rolled his eyes with utter disdain. His lips twitched as if mouthing a silent curse, yet he plastered on a look of naive confusion. “Then, Daozhang, where is this friend now? You’ve ended up like this—how come he hasn't come looking for you?”

Wei Wuxian felt a cold prickle of anger.What a venomous little dagger.

Predictably, Xiao Xingchen fell silent. Even A-Qing, oblivious to the history, picked up on the sudden chill. Holding her breath, she shot Xue Yang a sharp glare, grinding her teeth as if itching to bite him. After drifting off in thought, Xiao Xingchen broke the quiet. “I don't know where he is right now. But I hope…”

He trailed off, gently patting A-Qing’s head instead. “All right, that’s enough for tonight. I really am terrible at stories; don't torture me any longer.”

A-Qing conceded obediently. “Oh. Okay then!”

Out of nowhere, Xue Yang chimed in. “How about I tell one?”

Sulking over the abrupt ending, A-Qing immediately perked up. “Fine, fine! Let's hear it.”

Xue Yang leaned back leisurely. “Once upon a time, there was a little kid.

“This kid had a massive sweet tooth. But he had no parents, no home, and no money, so he almost never got any sweets. One day, he was sitting on some steps zoning out, just like always. Across the street was a tavern, and a man sitting at one of the tables noticed him and waved him over.”

The opening was hardly a masterpiece, but it was miles better than Xiao Xingchen’s dry history lesson. If A-Qing had rabbit ears, they’d be standing at full attention right now.

Xue Yang went on: “The kid was clueless, with nothing better to do, so the moment someone waved, he bolted straight over. The man pointed at a plate of pastries on the table and asked him, ‘Want some?’

“Of course he wanted some. He nodded like crazy. So the man handed the kid a slip of paper and said, ‘Deliver this to a certain room at a certain place, and when you get back, the pastries are yours.’

“The kid was thrilled. Run an errand, get a plate of sweets—earned with his own two hands.

“He couldn't read. He grabbed the paper and ran off to the address. A burly brute opened the door, glanced at the note, and instantly backhanded the kid so hard blood gushed from his nose. He grabbed the kid by the hair and barked, ‘Who told you to bring this filth to me?!’”

That kid was Xue Yang himself.

Wei Wuxian hadn't expected someone so conniving now to have been so naive back then—doing whatever he was told. Whatever was written on that paper had to be vile. The coward at the tavern likely had a grudge against the brute and didn't dare pick a fight himself, using a street urchin as a messenger to deliver the insult instead. Utterly pathetic.

Xue Yang continued, “Terrified, the kid pointed the way. The brute dragged him by the hair all the way back to the tavern, but the coward had already bolted. Even the leftovers on the table had been cleared away by the waiter. Enraged, the brute flipped a bunch of tables, cursed up a storm, and stormed off.

“The kid was desperate. He’d run the errand, taken a beating, and had his hair yanked so hard his scalp felt peeled raw. Going through all that and not getting his sweets was unacceptable. With tears welling in his eyes, he asked the waiter, ‘Where are my pastries? The man promised me my pastries!’”

A wide, cheerful grin spread across Xue Yang’s face. “The waiter had just seen his shop trashed and was fuming. He slapped the kid right out the door—several ringing blows that left his ears buzzing. The kid picked himself up and wandered down the street, and guess what? What a coincidence. He ran right into the man who gave him the letter.”

He stopped right there. Completely hooked, A-Qing urged, “And then what? What happened?!”

“What else could happen?” Xue Yang drawled. “Just took a few more slaps and kicks.”

A-Qing pointed at him. “That was you, wasn't it?! The sweet tooth—it has to be you! How could you be so useless as a kid? If it were me, I’d spit all over his food and tea first, and then beat him black and blue—” Flailing her arms in indignation, she nearly clipped Xiao Xingchen.

“All right, that’s enough,” Xiao Xingchen intervened, stepping in. “Storytime’s over. Time for bed.”

As Xiao Xingchen lifted her into her makeshift bed inside the coffin, A-Qing was still pounding her chest in frustration. “Ugh! Both of your stories sucked! One was boring enough to kill me, and the other was infuriating enough to make me explode! God, that tavern jerk makes my blood boil!”

Tucking the blanket around her, Xiao Xingchen took a few steps and asked softly, “What happened after that?”

“Take a guess,” Xue Yang retorted. “There is no after. Didn't your story cut off early, too?”

Xiao Xingchen said gently, “Whatever happened afterward, you are safe and sound now. There is no need to dwell on the past.”

“I’m not dwelling on anything,” Xue Yang scoffed. “It’s just that little blind brat keeps stealing all my candies. She ate the last one, and it reminded me of when I couldn't get any.”

A-Qing kicked the wooden side of the coffin hard in protest. “Don't listen to his lies, Daozhang! I barely ate any!”

Xiao Xingchen let out a soft laugh. “Get some rest, both of you.”

That night, Xue Yang didn't tag along. Xiao Xingchen headed out on a night-hunt alone, and while A-Qing lay safely in her coffin, she stared wide-awake into the dark.

Just as the first pale light of dawn broke, Xiao Xingchen slipped back through the door, quiet as a ghost.

Passing the coffin, he reached his hand inside. A-Qing squeezed her eyes shut, faking sleep. Only after Xiao Xingchen stepped back outside the funeral home did she open them. Sitting right beside her straw pillow was a small piece of candy.

Poking her head up, she peeked toward the main room. Xue Yang wasn't asleep either; he sat at the table, lost in thought.

Right at the corner of the table lay a single piece of candy, sitting quietly in the dim light.

Ever since that night by the stove, Xiao Xingchen made a habit of handing each of them a piece of candy every single day. A-Qing was naturally thrilled. Xue Yang, on the other hand, neither thanked him nor turned it down—a nonchalant attitude that annoyed A-Qing for days.

Xiao Xingchen took full charge of their food and lodging in Yi City. Being blind, he couldn't tell fresh produce from spoiled, nor did he ever haggle. It was fine when he encountered kind vendors, but all too often dishonest peddlers took advantage of his blindness, shortchanging him on weight or offloading wilted scraps. Xiao Xingchen never minded—or simply never noticed—but A-Qing saw right through it. Boiling with fury, she insisted on tagging along to settle the score. Unfortunately, since she was pretending to be blind, she couldn't call them out directly, let alone flip their stalls in front of Xiao Xingchen.

That was where Xue Yang proved shockingly useful. True to his street-thug origins, he had sharp eyes and a razor tongue. Whenever he came along, he would shamelessly slash the asking price in half right out of the gate. If they agreed, he’d push his luck further; if they refused, his gaze would turn chillingly lethal. Terrified vendors quickly decided that gettinganymoney was a blessing and practically shoved the goods into his hands just to make him leave. Back when Xue Yang ran rampant across Kuizhou and Lanling, he’d probably never paid for a damn thing in his life. Seeing the dishonest vendors get a taste of their own medicine cheered A-Qing up so much that she even tossed a few grudging compliments his way. Between that and the daily sweet, a fragile, bizarre peace settled between them for a brief while.

Still, she could never truly shake her suspicion. That fragile truce was repeatedly swallowed up by lingering doubts.

One afternoon, A-Qing was wandering the streets, playing her blind-girl routine—a game she’d played her whole life and never grew tired of. Tapping her bamboo pole along the dirt, a voice suddenly called out from behind:

“Little girl, if you cannot see, you shouldn't walk so quickly.”

It was a young man’s voice, cool and somewhat distant. A-Qing turned. A few paces away stood a tall, slender cultivator robed in black, a long sword strapped across his back and a horsetail whisk resting in the crook of his arm. With his flowing robes, impeccable posture, and proud, solitary aura, he carried an undeniable air of lofty elegance.

It was Song Lan.

A-Qing tilted her head. Song Lan stepped forward, gently guiding her to the side with the whisk. “Fewer people walk by the roadside.”

Wei Wuxian couldn't help thinking:Xiao Xingchen’s soulmate through and through. Birds of a feather—only men of the exact same moral fiber could be that close.

A-Qing beamed. “Thank you, Daozhang!”

Song Lan drew the whisk back, sweeping his gaze over her. “Do not wander recklessly. The yin energy here is heavy; do not linger outside after sunset.”

“Got it!”

Nodding, Song Lan turned to leave. A-Qing couldn't resist watching him go. After a short distance, he stopped a passerby. “Excuse me. Have you seen a blind cultivator carrying a sword around here?”

A-Qing’s ears perked instantly.

“Not sure, Daozhang,” the passerby replied. “Maybe try asking further up the road.”

“Thank you.”

Tapping her bamboo pole, A-Qing trotted over. “Daozhang, why are you looking for him?”

Song Lan spun around. “You have seen him?”

“Maybe I have, maybe I haven't,” A-Qing played coy.

Song Lan pressed, “What will it take for you to remember?”

“Answer a few questions, and maybe it’ll jog my memory,” she countered. “Are you his friend?”

Song Lan froze. A heavy beat passed before he managed, “…Yes.”

Why the hesitation?Wei Wuxian wondered.

A-Qing noticed the reluctant tone too, her suspicions flaring. “Do you really know him? How tall is he? Is he handsome or ugly? What does his sword look like?”

Song Lan answered without missing a beat: “He is about my height, remarkably handsome, and his sword bears a carved frost-flower motif.”

Seeing that his description was spot-on and that he didn't look like a bad person, A-Qing relented. “I know where he is. Come with me, Daozhang!”

Song Lan had clearly spent years searching for his friend, weathered by countless dead ends. Finally catching wind of his whereabouts, he could barely process it, struggling to maintain his composure. “…Th-thank you…”

She led him toward the funeral home, but Song Lan stopped dead in his tracks several yards away. A-Qing glanced back. “What's wrong? Aren't you going in?”

For some reason, Song Lan had gone completely pale. He stared at the front doors as if dying to charge in, yet utterly paralyzed by fear—all of his aloof composure shattered.Is it stage fright? The fear of finally finding what you've been searching for?Wei Wuxian mused.

Just as Song Lan finally gathered the nerve to move, a languid figure strolled past and slipped through the front door ahead of him.

The moment he saw who it was, Song Lan’s face drained from pale white to sickly green.

Laughter drifted out from inside the hall. A-Qing scrunched her nose. “Ugh, the jerk is back.”

Song Lan demanded, “Who is that? Why is he here?!”

“Just some rotten scoundrel,” A-Qing grumbled. “He never gave his name, so who knows? Daozhang saved him. He clings to Daozhang all day—annoying as hell!”

Song Lan’s face twisted in an agonizing mix of shock and rage. A beat later, he hissed, “Quiet!”

Frightened by his expression, A-Qing shut her mouth instantly. Like shadows, the two slipped up to the funeral home wall—one standing by the window frame, the other crouching beneath the sill.

Inside, Xiao Xingchen’s voice sounded: “Whose turn is it today?”

The moment the voice hit his ears, Song Lan trembled so violently that even A-Qing noticed.

Xue Yang drawled, “How about we ditch taking turns? Let’s try something new.”

“You always have an excuse whenever it’s your turn,” Xiao Xingchen chuckled helplessly. “What new way?”

“Look, I’ve got two twigs here,” Xue Yang said. “Draw the long one, you stay. Draw the short one, you go. Deal?”

A beat of silence followed, then Xue Yang burst out laughing. “Yours is short! I win, you’re up!”

Xiao Xingchen sighed. “All right, I’ll go.”

Footsteps rustled as he got up to head toward the door. Wei Wuxian silently rooted:Yes, come outside! The second you step out, Song Lan can grab you and run!

Before Xiao Xingchen could take more than a few steps, Xue Yang called out, “Come back. I’ll go.”

Xiao Xingchen stopped. “Changed your mind already?”

Xue Yang pushed himself up. “Are you stupid? I tricked you. I drew the short one, but I had a third, longer twig hidden up my sleeve the whole time. No matter which one you picked, mine was always going to be longer. Just taking advantage of your blindness.”

After mocking Xiao Xingchen a bit more, he casually picked up the basket and strolled out the front door. A-Qing looked up at Song Lan, bewildered by why the tall cultivator was shaking with such volcanic rage. Song Lan gestured for her to stay quiet, leading her away in dead silence before demanding, “When did Xing… when did that Daozhang save him?”

His voice was dead serious. Picking up on the gravity, A-Qing answered somberly, “A long time ago. Almost a couple of years now.”

“Does he still not know who that man is?”

“Nope. No idea.”

“What has that man been doing around him all this time?”

“Running his mouth, picking on me, scaring me,” A-Qing listed. “And… oh, going on night-hunts with Daozhang!”

Song Lan’s brow snapped together. He knew damn well Xue Yang wasn't the charitable type. “Night-hunts? Hunting what? Do you know?”

Not daring to be careless, A-Qing thought hard. “A while back, they hunted walking corpses a lot. Nowadays, it’s mostly just wandering spirits, restless livestock, that sort of thing.”

Song Lan cross-examined her relentlessly, sensing foul play at every turn yet unable to put his finger on the exact thread. “Are they… close?”

Loath as she was to admit it, A-Qing confessed, “I think Daozhang gets lonely on his own… It’s rare for him to have company on the road. So… he seems to genuinely enjoy that jerk’s jokes…”

A dark cloud descended over Song Lan’s face, warring between unbridled fury and unbearable heartbreak. Through the roaring chaos in his mind, only one thought rang crystal clear:

Xiao Xingchen must never find out about this.

“Do not breathe a word of this to him,” Song Lan ordered coldly.

With that, he turned on his heel, storming off in the direction Xue Yang had gone. A-Qing called out after him, “Daozhang, are you going to beat that jerk up?!”

Song Lan was already tearing down the road. Wei Wuxian thought grimly:Beat him up? He’s going to skin Xue Yang alive.

Knowing Xue Yang had left with the market basket, A-Qing knew the route he’d take. Taking a shortcut through the woods, she sprinted like the wind, her heart hammering against her ribs. After chasing for a while, Xue Yang’s figure finally appeared ahead. Swapping a basket brimming with greens, radishes, and steamed buns to one hand, he ambled along, yawning lazily—clearly on his casual stroll back from the market.

A-Qing was an expert at sneaking around and eavesdropping. She crept through the brush at the edge of the woods, shadowing him step for step. Suddenly, Song Lan’s icy voice cut through the trees ahead:

“Xue Yang.”

It was like a bucket of ice water dumped over his head, or a vicious slap knocking him awake from a dead sleep. Xue Yang’s expression turned utterly foul in an instant.

Song Lan stepped out from behind an old tree. His sword was already drawn, the cold point angling toward the dirt.

Feigning surprise, Xue Yang drawled, “Well, well, if it isn't Daozhang Song! What a rare guest. Dropping by for dinner?”

Song Lan lunged, his blade thrusting forward in a lethal strike. With a metallic hiss, Xue Yang flicked Jiangzai from his sleeve to parry the blow. He skidded back several paces, set his basket down by a tree trunk, and spat, “You damned priest. I finally get in the mood to go grocery shopping for once, and you show up to ruin my day!”

Consumed by a volcanic rage, Song Lan pressed him with killing strikes, every move aimed straight for the throat. “What filthy games are you playing at?!” he hissed. “What do you want with Xiao Xingchen?!”

Xue Yang chuckled. “And here I was wondering why Daozhang Song was holding back. So that's what you want to know.”

“Speak!” Song Lan roared. “A scumbag like you, helping him night-hunt out of the goodness of your heart?!”

A blade of sword-glare grazed Xue Yang’s cheek, drawing a thin line of red. He didn't even flinch. “I'm touched. You really do know me best, Daozhang Song!”

One was classically trained in the purest orthodox Daoist arts; the other was a street-brawler whose vicious style had been forged in arson and murder. Song Lan’s swordsmanship was clearly superior. With a sharp twist of his wrist, his blade drove clean through Xue Yang’s arm. “Talk!”

If he hadn't needed answers so desperately, that strike wouldn't have landed in the shoulder—it would have torn right through Xue Yang’s neck. With a steel blade embedded in his flesh, Xue Yang’s expression didn't even waver. “You really want to hear it? I'm worried you'll lose your mind. Trust me, some things are better left unsaid.”

Song Lan’s voice dripped ice. “Xue Yang, my patience is wearing thin!”

Clang!

Xue Yang knocked away a thrust aimed directly at his eyes. “Fine, fine, you asked for it. You want to know what your dear Daoist friend, your cherished confidant has been up to? He's been slaughtering walking corpses. Slaying demons, purging evil, expecting nothing in return—it's so noble it brings a tear to my eye. Sure, he scooped out his own eyes for you and ended up blind, but lucky for him, Shuanghua points straight to corpse energy. Even better: I figured out that if you just cut out the tongues of poisoned villagers so they can't talk, Shuanghua can't tell the living apart from the dead. So…”

He laid it all out, in agonizing, meticulous detail. Song Lan began to tremble—from his fingertips down to the edge of his blade. “You monster… You absolute, inhuman monster…”

“You know, Daozhang Song,” Xue Yang remarked, “cultured gentlemen like you are at a real disadvantage in a fight. Every time you get mad, it’s always the same three insults—boring, toothless, zero sting. I stopped calling people ‘monsters’ when I was seven.”

Blind with fury, Song Lan drove his sword straight for the throat once more. “He cannot see! How could you deceive him like this?!”

The blow was fast and vicious. Xue Yang barely dodged, the blade shearing through his collarbone. He didn't even wince, as if he couldn't feel a thing. “He cannot see? Tell me, Daozhang Song, who did he gouge his eyes out for in the first place? Have you forgotten?”

Song Lan froze mid-strike, all the color draining from his face.

Xue Yang pressed on, his voice dripping poison. “What right do you have to judge me? As his friend? Do you have the nerve to call yourself Xiao Xingchen’s friend? Hahaha! Need me to jog your memory, Daozhang Song? After I slaughtered Baixue Temple, what were the exact words you threw in his face? He came to you sick with worry, wanting to help—how did you look at him? What did you say to him?”

Song Lan’s mind spun into chaos. “I—back then, I—”

Xue Yang cut him off ruthlessly. “You were drowning in grief? In pain? In misery? Desperate for a punching bag, so you took it out on him? To be fair, I only wiped out your temple because of him, so it makes total sense you blamed him. It played right into my hands, honestly.”

Every word was a poisoned needle striking a nerve.

Xue Yang closed the distance with both blade and tongue, his strikes growing smoother, deadlier, and far more vicious until he had subtly seized the upper hand. Song Lan didn't even notice.

“Tell me, who was the one who said,‘I never want to see you again’?” Xue Yang mocked. “Wasn't that you, Daozhang Song? He gave you what you wanted—he carved his eyes out for you and disappeared from your life. So why the hell are you here now? Aren't you just making things awkward for everyone? Isn't that right, Daozhang Xiao Xingchen?”

Song Lan gasped, his sword faltering mid-air.

It was the oldest trick in the book, but his mind had been shattered, his focus completely undone. Xue Yang didn't waste a heartbeat. With a flick of his sleeve, a cloud of corpse powder burst into the air.

No one had ever encountered this refined venom before. Song Lan breathed in several lungfuls before he could react, instantly hacking and choking. Jiangzai had been waiting. A flash of cold steel darted forward, thrusting brutally straight into his open mouth.

Darkness swallowed Wei Wuxian’s vision. A-Qing had squeezed her eyes shut in sheer terror.

Even without seeing, he knew. That was the moment Song Lan’s tongue had been severed.

The sound alone was sickening.

Tears welled in A-Qing’s eyes, but she bit her lip until it bled, refusing to let out a sound. Trembling, she forced her eyes open. Song Lan was leaning heavily on his sword to keep from collapsing, one hand clamped over his mouth as crimson gushed between his fingers.

Crippled by the ambush and the agonizing loss of his tongue, Song Lan could barely stand. Yet he ripped his sword from the dirt and lurched toward Xue Yang in one last, desperate strike. Xue Yang sidestepped it with ease, a sickening grin plastered across his face.

A heartbeat later, Wei Wuxian realized what that smile meant.

A flash of silver light burst straight through Song Lan’s chest, the tip emerging through his back.

Song Lan looked down, watching the pristine blade of Shuanghua pierce clean through his heart. Slowly, he raised his head to see Xiao Xingchen holding the hilt, his face serene and calm.

Completely oblivious, Xiao Xingchen called out, “Are you there?”

Song Lan’s lips moved, soundless.

Xue Yang smiled warmly. “I'm here. What brought you out?”

Xiao Xingchen pulled Shuanghua free and slid it back into its scabbard. “Shuanghua stirred. I followed its guidance to check it out.” He sounded puzzled. “It’s been a long time since I've encountered a walking corpse around here. And a solitary one, too—did it wander in from elsewhere?”

Slowly, Song Lan dropped to his knees before him.

Xue Yang looked down at him from above. “Must have. It was growling like crazy.”

In this moment, all Song Lan had to do was place his sword into Xiao Xingchen’s hands. Xiao Xingchen would recognize it instantly—he knew his dearest friend’s blade by touch alone.

But Song Lan couldn't bring himself to do it. Hand his sword over, just to let Xiao Xingchen know he had just murdered his best friend with his own hands?

Xue Yang had counted on this very cruelty. He stood there, untouchable, savoring every second. “Come on, let’s get back and cook. I'm starving.”

“Did you get the groceries?” Xiao Xingchen asked.

“Got 'em. Just ran into this nasty thing on the way back. Rotten luck.”

Xiao Xingchen turned and took the lead. Xue Yang casually brushed at the blood on his shoulder and arm, picked up his basket, and paused as he stepped past Song Lan. Leaning down with a faint smile, he whispered:

“None for you.”

Only after Xue Yang was long gone—likely already back at the funerary hall with Xiao Xingchen—did A-Qing finally dare to rise from the bushes.

She had crouched so long her legs were completely numb. Leaning heavily on her bamboo pole, she limped forward, shaking from head to toe until she reached Song Lan’s rigid, kneeling corpse.

His eyes stared wide in death. A-Qing flinched at the sight, then saw the thick blood pooling beneath his chin, soaking his robes and the earth. Tears spilled down her cheeks.

Trembling, she reached out and gently closed his eyes. Dropping to her knees, she pressed her palms together. “Daozhang, please don't hold a grudge against me, or against that other Daozhang. If I had jumped in, I would've died too. I had to hide; I couldn't save you. The Daozhang was tricked by that evil freak—he didn't mean to, he had no idea it was you!”

Sobs racked her small frame. “I have to go back now. Please, if your spirit can hear me, watch over me. Help me get Daozhang Xiao Xingchen out of there. Help us escape that monster's clutches, and let that demon Xue Yang die a dog's death—hacked into a thousand pieces, cursed for eternity!”

She bowed deeply, knocking her forehead against the dirt three times. Wiping her face clean with the back of her sleeve, she took a deep breath, braced herself, and headed back toward Yi City.

By the time she returned to the funerary hall, night had fallen. Xue Yang was sitting by the table peeling apples, carving them into little rabbit shapes, looking thoroughly pleased with himself. Anyone seeing him would have pegged him as nothing more than a mischievous youth, never dreaming of the butchery he had just carried out. Xiao Xingchen emerged carrying a plate of stir-fried greens. Hearing the door, he said, “A-Qing? Where did you run off to today? You're back so late.”

Xue Yang glanced her way, his eyes suddenly narrowing to needlepoints. “What happened to her? Her eyes are all swollen.”

Xiao Xingchen hurried over, concerned. “What's wrong? Did someone pick on you?”

“Pick on her?” Xue Yang snorted. “Who could possibly bully her?”

Though a smile remained on his face, his suspicion was plainly aroused. Without warning, A-Qing slammed her bamboo pole to the ground and burst into noisy, wailing tears.

Snot and tears streamed down her face as she threw herself into Xiao Xingchen’s arms, sobbing breathlessly, “Wahhh! Am I ugly?! Am I that ugly?! Daozhang, tell me, am I really hideous?!”

Xiao Xingchen patted her head soothingly. “Of course not. Our A-Qing is lovely. Who called you ugly?”

Xue Yang made a face. “Ugly as sin. Even uglier when you bawl.”

Xiao Xingchen chided him softly, “Don't be like that.”

A-Qing wailed even louder, stomping her feet. “Daozhang, you can't even see! What's the point of you saying I'm pretty? You're just lying to make me feel better!Hecan see, andhesays I'm ugly! I really must be disgusting! Ugly and blind!”

With this little tantrum, both men naturally assumed some neighborhood brats had mocked her on the street, calling her an ugly freak or a blind hag, and hurt her feelings. Xue Yang scoffed, “Someone calls you ugly and you run home to cry? Where did all your usual venom go?”

“You're the venomous one!” A-Qing snapped, turning back to Xiao Xingchen. “Daozhang, do you have any money left?”

Xiao Xingchen paused, slightly sheepish. “Um… I think we have a little.”

Xue Yang cut in, “I've got money. I can lend you some.”

A-Qing spat in his direction. “You've been freeloading off us for years, and now you want tolendme a few coins?! Cheapskate! Shameless bastard! Daozhang, I want to buy pretty clothes and nice jewelry. Will you come with me?”

Ah,Wei Wuxian realized.She’s trying to lure Xiao Xingchen out. But what if Xue Yang insists on tagging along?

Xiao Xingchen replied, “I can go with you, of course, but I won't be able to tell if they suit you.”

Xue Yang chimed in again, “I can look for her.”

A-Qing jumped up so fast her head nearly bumped Xiao Xingchen’s chin. “I don't care, I don't care! I only want you to come! I don't want him anywhere near me! All he does is call me ugly and make fun of my eyes!”

Her bouts of unreasonable petulance were a regular occurrence, and both men were used to it. Xue Yang pulled a face at her, while Xiao Xingchen yielded. “All right. How about tomorrow?”

“I want to go tonight!”

Xue Yang drawled, “The market's already closed. Where are you going to buy anything this late?”

Cornered, A-Qing huffed, “Fine! Tomorrow! You promised!”

With her first plan foiled, throwing another fit to leave right now would only make Xue Yang more suspicious. A-Qing had no choice but to sit down at the table to eat. Though her performance had been flawless and natural, her stomach had been knotted with terror the entire time. Even now, the hand holding her bowl trembled faintly. Xue Yang sat directly to her left, his sidelong gaze skimming over her, making the muscles in her calves lock up tight. Paralyzed with fear, she couldn't swallow a bite. Using her fake anger as a cover, she spat out every mouthful, furiously stabbing at her rice and muttering under her breath, “Dead bitch, rotten brat, like you're any prize pig yourself. Bitch!”

Listening to her curse out this imaginary girl, Xue Yang rolled his eyes, while Xiao Xingchen scolded gently, “Don't waste food.”

Xue Yang’s gaze drifted away from A-Qing, settling quietly on Xiao Xingchen across the table.No wonder the little delinquent can mimic Xiao Xingchen so well,Wei Wuxian thought.Sitting across from him day after day gave him plenty of time to study every single gesture.

Xiao Xingchen remained oblivious to the eyes fixed upon him. At the end of the day, in this entire room, he was the only one who was truly blind.

Once dinner ended, Xiao Xingchen gathered the bowls and headed to the back. A-Qing, squirming on her seat, tried to slip in after him, but Xue Yang’s voice suddenly rang out:

“A-Qing.”

Her heart jumped into her throat. Wei Wuxian could feel the hairs standing up on the back of her neck.

She whirled around. “Why are you using my name all of a sudden?!”

“Didn't you say you hated being called a blind brat?” Xue Yang asked evenly.

A-Qing crossed her arms. “Nobody acts nice without an angle! What do you want?”

Xue Yang gave a pleasant smile. “Nothing much. Just giving you some advice on how to handle it next time someone curses at you.”

“Oh yeah? Like what?”

“Next time someone calls you ugly,” Xue Yang said smoothly, “cut her face up with seventeen or eighteen slashes. Make sure she’s too hideous to ever show her face in public again. And if someone calls you blind, sharpen the tip of that bamboo cane of yours and shove it right into both of her eyes. Turn her blind, too. Let's see if she dares run her mouth after that.”

A chilling dread crept down A-Qing’s spine. Forcing herself to act like she thought he was just spinning tall tales to freak her out, she scoffed, “You're just trying to scare me again!”

Xue Yang snickered. “Believe whatever you like.” He pushed the plate of rabbit-carved apples toward her. “Eat up.”

Staring at the plate of sweet, delicately carved apple bunnies, a deep, bone-chilling dread settled over both A-Qing and Wei Wuxian.

The next morning, A-Qing woke up early, raising hell for Xiao Xingchen to take her out shopping for pretty robes and rouge. Xue Yang grumbled, “If both of you are leaving, am I on grocery duty again?”

A-Qing shot back, “What's wrong with you buying groceries for once? Daozhang's done it a million times! You're the only cheat who plays tricks to get out of doing your share!”

“Fine, fine,” Xue Yang said casually. “I'll go. Going right now.”

The moment the front door closed behind him, Xiao Xingchen asked, “A-Qing, aren't you ready yet? Shall we go?”

A-Qing peeked out to ensure Xue Yang was truly gone. Then she stepped back inside, pulled the door firmly shut, and asked in a shaking voice:

“Daozhang… do you know someone named Xue Yang?”
